text.en: Ravi runs 100 m in 20 seconds and Meena in 18 seconds. Who is faster? To compare, we measure time and work out speed.

Long ago people measured time with the Sun, sundials and water clocks. Today we use clocks and watches. The SI unit of time is the second. 60 seconds make 1 minute and 60 minutes make 1 hour.
A pendulum is a small mass hung by a thread that swings back and forth. One complete to-and-fro swing is an oscillation. The time taken for one oscillation is its time period. For a given pendulum the time period is almost the same each time, so pendulums were used in clocks.
Speed tells how fast an object moves. Speed equals distance divided by time. If a car covers 120 km in 2 hours its speed is 60 km per hour. Speed is measured in metres per second or kilometres per hour.
A distance-time graph shows how far an object has gone as time passes. A straight slanted line shows steady speed. A flat line shows the object is at rest.

Watch where a post’s shadow falls at different times on a clear day. A sundial uses that changing position to mark the time.
In a water clock, the changing water level can mark elapsed time. A useful clock needs a change that repeats or progresses predictably.
Ten could mean ten seconds or ten minutes. Write the unit with every reading so somebody else can use it.
There are sixty seconds in a minute. Multiply sixty by two to express two minutes in seconds.
Change the minutes to seconds first. Then add the fifteen seconds to get a total of one hundred and thirty-five seconds.
A simple model has a fixed pivot, a light string and a small mass called the bob. The bob swings about its usual hanging position.
Release the bob from one side. It moves to the other side and comes back. Count one oscillation when it returns to its starting side.
Starting a stopwatch can add a small timing error. Measure ten complete swings, then divide the time by ten.
If ten swings take eighteen seconds, the mean time per oscillation is one point eight seconds.
Compare two pendulums of different lengths. Use similar small swings and the same method of timing so the comparison tests the effect of length.

board.text: Change one thing at a time

text.en: A longer pendulum generally takes more time for each small swing. Check that prediction by timing ten swings of each model.
For the same distance, the runner who takes less time is faster. Eight seconds beats ten seconds over forty metres.

board.text: 40 m in 8 s vs 40 m in 10 s

text.en: When the times match, the runner who covers more distance is faster. Twenty-four metres is greater than eighteen in the same six seconds.

board.text: 24 m in 6 s vs 18 m in 6 s

text.en: What if both distance and time differ? Divide each distance by its time and compare speeds in the same unit.
A runner covers fifty metres in ten seconds. The runner covers five metres per second on average.
Seventy-two kilometres are seventy-two thousand metres, and one hour is three thousand six hundred seconds. Divide to get twenty metres per second.
At four metres per second for six seconds, the distance is four times six, or twenty-four metres. Check the units before multiplying.
At four metres per second, travelling thirty-two metres takes eight seconds. Thirty-two divided by four equals eight.
Along a straight path, a vehicle that covers six metres every second has uniform linear motion.
Three equal time intervals with different distances show non-uniform motion. This vehicle speeds up.

board.text: 2 m, then 4 m, then 6 m each second

text.en: A scooter pauses at a junction. Its distance travelled stays the same during the pause, then increases when it moves again.
Walk thirty metres in ten seconds, then wait ten seconds. The average over the full twenty seconds is one point five metres per second.

board.text: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time

problem.en: A cyclist covers 36 km in 3 hours. Find the speed.

text.en: Speed is distance divided by time.
36 divided by 3 is 12 km per hour.

problem.en: A pendulum completes 15 oscillations in 24 seconds. Find its mean time period.

text.en: Divide 24 seconds by 15.

why.en: The period measures the time for one complete oscillation.

text.en: The mean is 1.6 seconds per oscillation.

why.en: Multiply 1.6 by 15 to check the total.

problem.en: A turtle travels 3 metres in each of three equal 60-second intervals along a straight line. Describe its motion.

text.en: Each equal interval adds the same distance.

why.en: The turtle shows uniform linear motion in this model.

text.en: Speed = 3 ÷ 60 = 0.05 metres per second.

why.en: Convert all intervals to a common unit before comparing.

prompt.en: Explain how you would compare the speed of two runners.

requiredIdeas.en: The shorter time means higher speed.

commonMisconceptions.en: Using the longer time as faster.

points.en: Time is measured in seconds, minutes, hours.
A pendulum has a time period.
A flat line on a distance-time graph means rest.
